feed.title: What does "post-quantum" actually mean for a Bitcoin L2 when settlement still happens on a non-PQ L1?

entry.title: What does "post-quantum" actually mean for a Bitcoin L2 when settlement still happens on a non-PQ L1?
entry.summary:
The Lightning Network provides a mechanism for users to exit unilaterally from the network back to the blockchain, known as the ultimate peg-out. This process serves as a final recourse when the value of tokens within a Lightning channel drops below that of their onchain equivalents. However, the standard configuration enforces a two-week delay for such unilateral exits, effectively rate-limiting the withdrawal from the Lightning Network. This restriction results in Lightning Network tokens generally holding a slightly lower average value compared to blockchain tokens.
Services such as Lightning Loop and Boltz have historically observed a greater demand for Lightning-to-blockchain swaps than the reverse. Swaps function differently from pegs; they do not alter the supply of tokens or guarantee equivalence between systems. Instead, swap service providers accumulate tokens from one side and must eventually adjust prices, halt operations, or rely on a true peg mechanism to maintain economic balance. A genuine peg involves either the destruction or cryptographic locking of tokens in one system to generate or release tokens in another, directly affecting the usable token supply and enabling proper economic parity across networks. For a robust system, such pegging must be bidirectional.
The Lightning Network partially alleviates the constraints of unilateral exits by allowing mutual exits, which enable immediate withdrawals without the typical two-week waiting period. This feature helps maintain the effectiveness of the peg-out process, minimizing the value discrepancy between Lightning Network and onchain tokens. The small discount on Lightning Network tokens is often considered an acceptable tradeoff for the advantages of rapid, low-fee transfers, particularly for small amounts.
Despite these improvements, onboarding new users to the Lightning Network remains challenging due to the lingering disparity in value between Lightning Network and onchain tokens. Potential users are asked to exchange onchain tokens—perceived as more valuable—for Lightning Network tokens, with the assurance that the speed and convenience of Lightning will compensate for the minor loss in value. Overcoming this skepticism requires enhancements to the exit mechanism, specifically through implementation of a true peg-out rather than reliance on swap services.
If a second-layer solution is only partially pegged, swap services that facilitate L2-to-blockchain conversions may consistently face an imbalance, accumulating excess L2 tokens. If these tokens cannot be offloaded onto the market or destroyed via a secure peg that releases corresponding assets on the blockchain, such services will ultimately find it unsustainable to continue operations.
